variants.title: Validate in order
variants.context: Validate at the recipient’s boundary in a bounded profile: parse defensively; pin token type and an algorithm allowlist; select keys from trusted configuration bound to the issuer; verify the complete cryptographic operation; validate required claims; apply replay and authorization policy.
variants.prompt: An API receives a bearer JWT. Put the validation gates in order.

items.text: Resolve kid only within the key set bound to the configured issuer; ignore jku, jwk, and x5u from the header.
Parse defensively: reject malformed serialization, duplicate claims, unsupported critical headers, oversized input.
Validate exact issuer, intended audience, subject semantics, exp, and nbf.
Pin the expected typ and pass an explicit algorithm allowlist; never accept none.
Apply replay and authorization policy: audience restriction, sender constraint, revocation, application checks.
Verify the complete signature, MAC, or decryption; reject the whole object on any failure.

variants.hint: Nothing about the claims is trusted before the cryptographic operation passes.
variants.explanation: Parse → pin → select keys → verify → validate claims → authorize. Data inside an unverified token is attacker-controlled input.

variants.title: Validate in order
variants.context: Validate at the recipient’s boundary in a bounded profile: parse defensively; pin token type and an algorithm allowlist; select keys from trusted configuration bound to the issuer; verify the complete cryptographic operation; validate required claims; apply replay and authorization policy.
variants.prompt: A token arrives with an unexpected jku header pointing at an attacker’s server. Put the correct handling in order.

items.text: The request is rejected before application code runs.
Ignore jku and resolve the key only from the issuer-bound key set; if kid is unknown, fail.
Pin the type and algorithm allowlist.

variants.hint: Key discovery comes from configuration, not from the token.
variants.explanation: Do not blindly follow key URLs from an untrusted header.

variants.title: Validate in order
variants.context: Validate at the recipient’s boundary in a bounded profile: parse defensively; pin token type and an algorithm allowlist; select keys from trusted configuration bound to the issuer; verify the complete cryptographic operation; validate required claims; apply replay and authorization policy.
variants.prompt: A copied bearer token passes every cryptographic and claim check. Put the gates in order, ending with what still applies.

items.text: Validate issuer, audience, and time window.
Apply replay policy and sender constraint; a valid token is still a bearer credential.

variants.hint: A valid signature does not prove the presenter is the intended holder.
variants.explanation: Use audience restriction, sender constraint, one-time state, and revocation according to the threat.

variants.title: Read the structure
variants.context: A JWS compact JWT has three parts and a readable payload; a valid signature shows the bytes match a trusted key, not that the application permits anything. A JWE has five parts and provides confidentiality. Base64url is not encryption.
variants.prompt: A three-part JWT’s payload is readable in the browser. Is that a bug?
options: Yes; a working signature would keep the payload opaque.
No. A JWS payload is readable and not encrypted.
Yes; any token held in a browser must be encrypted.
optionFeedback: Signing covers integrity only. A readable payload is the normal JWS shape, not a broken signature.
Signing protects integrity, not secrecy.
Confidentiality needs a JWE, and it is required only when the payload itself is sensitive.
variants.explanation: A signed token is not a secret container.

variants.title: Read the structure
variants.context: A JWS compact JWT has three parts and a readable payload; a valid signature shows the bytes match a trusted key, not that the application permits anything. A JWE has five parts and provides confidentiality. Base64url is not encryption.
variants.prompt: A token has five base64url parts. What is it?
options: Two JWTs concatenated by a broken client.
A JWE compact serialization, which is encrypted.
A malformed JWS with two extra segments.
optionFeedback: Five parts is the JWE shape, not two tokens joined together.
Protected header, encrypted key, IV, ciphertext, and tag.
The part count comes from the JOSE structure, and five parts is a well-formed JWE.
variants.hint: How many parts does each JOSE structure have?
variants.explanation: JWE is a separate encrypted representation.

variants.title: Read the structure
variants.context: A JWS compact JWT has three parts and a readable payload; a valid signature shows the bytes match a trusted key, not that the application permits anything. A JWE has five parts and provides confidentiality. Base64url is not encryption.
variants.prompt: A signature verifies against a trusted key. Does that grant the request permission?
options: Yes; a trusted key is the authorization decision.
Yes, provided aud names this resource server.
No. Integrity is proven; authorization is separate.
optionFeedback: Verification proves who minted the token, not what the caller may do with it.
Audience is another gate; authorization is still separate.
Integrity is not authority.
variants.hint: Which question does a signature answer?
variants.explanation: JWT is a format, not a complete security system.

variants.title: Interpret the claim
variants.context: iss must match the configured issuer exactly and bind verification keys; aud must name this resource server; sub is an identifier in the issuer’s namespace, not automatically a username or permission; exp, nbf, and iat are seconds since the epoch.
variants.prompt: A token’s aud names a different API. Should this API accept it?
options: No; a resource server rejects tokens that do not name it.
Yes, because the issuer is one this API already trusts.
Yes, as long as the token has not expired yet.
optionFeedback: Audience restriction stops tokens minted for one API being replayed at another.
Issuer trust says the token is genuine, not that it was minted for this API.
Expiry is a separate check. A live token addressed to another API is still a replay here.
variants.hint: Was this token minted for this recipient?

variants.title: Interpret the claim
variants.context: iss must match the configured issuer exactly and bind verification keys; aud must name this resource server; sub is an identifier in the issuer’s namespace, not automatically a username or permission; exp, nbf, and iat are seconds since the epoch.
variants.prompt: An application uses sub directly as its database primary key and permission level. What is wrong?
options: sub should have been read from the aud claim.
sub names the subject inside the issuer’s namespace.
Nothing; sub is stable and unique per user.
optionFeedback: aud names the recipient of the token, not the subject it describes.
Map subjects deliberately and derive permissions from application policy.
Stability does not make it authority. Permissions come from application policy, not from an identifier.
variants.hint: What does sub promise, and what does it not?
variants.explanation: Received claims are untrusted lookup input.

variants.title: Interpret the claim
variants.context: iss must match the configured issuer exactly and bind verification keys; aud must name this resource server; sub is an identifier in the issuer’s namespace, not automatically a username or permission; exp, nbf, and iat are seconds since the epoch.
variants.prompt: A private claim named role is present. What does it mean?
options: Administrator access, as the claim name implies.
Whatever the JWT library maps that claim to.
Only whatever the issuer and this recipient agreed.
optionFeedback: The string carries no universal semantics. Only an agreed profile gives it meaning.
Libraries parse claims; they do not define application meaning.
Private claims need collision-resistant names or a closed agreement.
variants.explanation: An application profile defines required claims and acceptable values.

variants.title: Stop the attack
variants.context: Attacks target the verifier’s policy: alg=none, RSA-to-HMAC confusion, a foreign issuer, the wrong audience, an attacker-controlled key URL in jku or x5u, or a copied bearer token.
variants.prompt: A token arrives with alg set to none. What stops it?
options: An algorithm allowlist that never includes none.
Raising the RSA signing key to 4096 bits.
Checking exp and nbf before the signature.
optionFeedback: The verifier chooses the allowlist; the token does not.
An alg=none token carries no signature at all, so key length never enters the check.
Time checks bound how long a token lives; they never test whether it was signed.
variants.hint: Who decides which algorithms are acceptable?
variants.explanation: This API profile never accepts none.

variants.title: Stop the attack
variants.context: Attacks target the verifier’s policy: alg=none, RSA-to-HMAC confusion, a foreign issuer, the wrong audience, an attacker-controlled key URL in jku or x5u, or a copied bearer token.
variants.prompt: An attacker signs a token with HMAC using the server’s RSA public key as the secret. What stops it?
options: Checking that the issuer claim still matches.
Pin the algorithm to the key so RSA cannot become HMAC.
Rotating the RSA key pair more frequently.
optionFeedback: The attack leaves the issuer claim untouched, so it matches and the token still passes.
Algorithm confusion is defeated by policy pinning.
A fresh public key is still public, so the attacker signs with the new one instead.
variants.hint: Can the token choose how it is verified?
variants.explanation: Bind keys to algorithms and issuers.

variants.title: Stop the attack
variants.context: Attacks target the verifier’s policy: alg=none, RSA-to-HMAC confusion, a foreign issuer, the wrong audience, an attacker-controlled key URL in jku or x5u, or a copied bearer token.
variants.prompt: A valid token issued by another trusted-looking provider arrives. What stops it?
options: Exact issuer matching with keys bound to that issuer.
Verifying the signature with any configured key.
Requiring the typ header to be set to JWT.
optionFeedback: A foreign issuer must fail the iss comparison and key binding.
A signature that verifies under some trusted key still says nothing about which issuer minted it.
typ pins the token kind, and a foreign issuer can set it just as easily.
variants.hint: Which issuer is configured, and which keys belong to it?

variants.title: Do the time math
variants.context: NumericDate claims are seconds since the Unix epoch. Keep clock tolerance small and deliberate; a token is valid from nbf until exp.
variants.prompt: A token has iat 1,700,000,000 and exp 1,700,000,900. What is its lifetime in seconds?

variants.title: Do the time math
variants.context: NumericDate claims are seconds since the Unix epoch. Keep clock tolerance small and deliberate; a token is valid from nbf until exp.
variants.prompt: exp is 1,700,000,900 and the recipient allows 30 seconds of clock tolerance. What is the latest epoch second at which the token is still accepted?

mistakes.feedback: Tolerance extends acceptance slightly past exp.

variants.title: Do the time math
variants.context: NumericDate claims are seconds since the Unix epoch. Keep clock tolerance small and deliberate; a token is valid from nbf until exp.
variants.prompt: The current time is 1,700,000,000 and nbf is 1,700,000,060. How many seconds until the token becomes valid?
variants.explanation: The token is not yet valid for 60 seconds; reject it until then.

mistakes.feedback: Answer the difference, not the timestamp.
